problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.problem: You get an array of lowercase strings. Put the words that are anagrams of each other (same letters, same counts, any order) into the same group. Return the groups in any order.

examples.explanation: "eat", "tea", "ate" use the same letters; "tan" and "nat" too; "bat" has no partner.
One empty string forms its own group.

problems.intuition: Two words are anagrams exactly when their letter counts are equal. So if we turn each word into a key built from its 26 letter counts, all anagrams get the same key and a HashMap groups them for us. Counting is O(k) per word, cheaper than sorting the word.
approach: Create map: key string -> list of words.
For each word s, fill cnt[26] with its letter counts.
Build the key by appending every count followed by '#' (the separator stops 1,11 and 11,1 from looking the same).
Add s to map[key] (create the list if missing).
Return all the lists in map.values().
dryRun: s = "eat": cnt a=1,e=1,t=1 -> key K1, map = {K1:[eat]}.
s = "tea": same counts -> key K1, map = {K1:[eat,tea]}.
s = "tan": a=1,n=1,t=1 -> key K2, map adds {K2:[tan]}.

complexity.time: O(n * k) where k is the max word length (plus 26 per word for the key)

edgeCases: Empty string: all counts 0, it still gets a valid key and its own group.
Duplicate words like "abc","abc": both go to the same list.
Words with same letters but different counts ("aab" vs "abb") get different keys, so they stay apart.
problems.takeaway: Grouping by 'same multiset of letters' means: build a canonical key (counts or sorted string) and use a HashMap.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.problem: You get the heads of two sorted linked lists. Splice their nodes together into one sorted list and return its head.

examples.explanation: Take the smaller head each time.
One empty list, return the other one.

problems.intuition: The merged list must start with the smaller of the two heads. After picking it, the rest is the same problem on smaller inputs: merge what is left. That is a natural recursion, and since we only relink existing nodes no extra nodes are made.
approach: If list1 is null return list2; if list2 is null return list1.
If list1.val <= list2.val: list1 is the head, set list1.next = merge(list1.next, list2), return list1.
Otherwise list2 is the head: list2.next = merge(list1, list2.next), return list2.
dryRun: merge([1,2,4],[1,3,4]): 1 <= 1, so list1 node 1 is head, recurse on ([2,4],[1,3,4]).
merge([2,4],[1,3,4]): 2 > 1, list2 node 1 is head, recurse on ([2,4],[3,4]).
merge([4],[4]): 4 <= 4, take list1's 4, recurse on (null,[4]) -> returns [4].

complexity.space: O(n + m) recursion stack (an iterative dummy-node version is O(1))

edgeCases: One list empty: returns the other list as is.
Equal values: <= keeps list1's node first, either order is valid.
All of one list smaller than the other: recursion walks one list then attaches the other.
problems.takeaway: Linked list merge: pick the smaller head, recurse (or use a dummy node and a tail pointer). Base of merge sort and Merge k Sorted Lists.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.problem: Find all unique triplets [a, b, c] from nums (using three different indices) with a + b + c = 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triplets.

examples.explanation: (-1)+0+1 = 0 and (-1)+(-1)+2 = 0. The two triplets using a different -1 are the same triplet, so it appears once.

problems.intuition: Sort first. Fix the first number nums[i]; now we need two numbers in the sorted part to the right that sum to -nums[i]. In a sorted range, two pointers solve that: if the sum is too small move l right, if too big move r left. Sorting also puts duplicates next to each other, so skipping equal neighbours removes duplicate triplets.
approach: Sort nums.
For i from 0 to n-3: if nums[i] > 0 break (all later numbers are positive too). If nums[i] == nums[i-1] skip it.
Set l = i+1, r = n-1. While l < r compute sum = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r].
sum == 0 -> add the triplet, move both pointers, then skip repeats of nums[l] and nums[r].
Return res.
dryRun: i=0 (-4): l=1,r=5: sum=-4-1+2=-3 <0 l++; all sums stay negative until l meets r. No triplet.

complexity.space: O(1) extra besides the output (sort uses O(log n))

edgeCases: All zeros [0,0,0,0]: added once, the skip loops remove repeats.
No answer like [1,2,3]: breaks early since nums[0] > 0.
Big values like -100000 + 50000 + 50000: fits easily in int.
problems.takeaway: k-Sum on an array: sort, fix one element, then two pointers on the rest; skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicates.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.problem: Each task is a letter A to Z and takes one time unit. The same letter must have at least n units between two runs (you can idle). Tasks can be done in any order. Return the minimum total time units.

examples.explanation: A -> B -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> A -> B. After A, two other slots must pass before A again.
A -> B -> C -> D -> A -> B. Enough different tasks, no idle needed.
A -> B -> idle -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> idle -> A -> B.

problems.intuition: The most frequent task decides the shape. If it appears max times, it creates max - 1 full blocks of length n + 1 (the task plus n gap slots), and then one last row. The last row holds every task that also has frequency max (maxCnt of them). Other tasks fit into the gaps. If there are so many tasks that the gaps overflow, no idle is needed and the answer is just tasks.length. So answer = max((max - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCnt, tasks.length).
approach: Count each letter in cnt[26] and track max, the highest count.
Count maxCnt = how many letters have count == max.
ans = (max - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCnt.
Return Math.max(ans, tasks.length).
edgeCases: n = 0: formula gives at most tasks.length, so answer = tasks.length.
Many distinct tasks (ABCDEFG, n=2): formula is small, tasks.length wins.
Several letters tied at max: maxCnt adds them to the last row.
problems.takeaway: Cooldown scheduling: think in frames of size n + 1 built around the most frequent item; answer is max(frame formula, total tasks).

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.problem: Return the minimum number of operations to turn word1 into word2, where one operation is insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character.

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse (replace 'h' with 'r'), rorse -> rose (remove 'r'), rose -> ros (remove 'e').

intention -> inention (remove 't'), inention -> enention (replace 'i' with 'e'), enention -> exention (replace 'n' with 'x'), exention -> exection (replace 'n' with 'c'), exection -> execution (insert 'u').

problems.intuition: Let dp[i][j] = answer for the first i chars of word1 and first j chars of word2. Look at the last chars. If they match, they cost nothing: dp[i-1][j-1]. If not, the last step was one of: replace (dp[i-1][j-1] + 1), delete from word1 (dp[i-1][j] + 1), or insert into word1 (dp[i][j-1] + 1). Take the min. Turning a prefix into the empty string costs its length, which gives the base row and column.
approach: m = word1.length(), n = word2.length(); make dp[m+1][n+1].
dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j.
For i in 1..m, j in 1..n: if word1[i-1] == word2[j-1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1].
Else dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Return dp[m][n].
dryRun: word1 = horse (m=5), word2 = ros (n=3). Row 0 = [0,1,2,3], column 0 = 0..5.

complexity.space: O(m * n) (can be cut to O(n) with two rows)

edgeCases: One empty: answer is the other length (all inserts or deletes), straight from the base row or column.
problems.takeaway: Two-string DP (edit distance, LCS): dp[i][j] over prefixes, decide by the last characters, base cases are the empty prefixes.
